POST-FORECLOSURE TENANT 90-DAY NOTICE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St., Los Angeles, CA · January 1, 2026

POST-FORECLOSURE TENANT NOTICE TO QUIT: INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE
This information sheet describes, in general terms, a California statutory tenant protection that applies after a residential property has been sold at a foreclosure sale: California Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b, which requires the purchaser or other successor in interest to give certain residential tenants a longer written notice to quit than the notice period that would otherwise apply, before an unlawful detainer action to remove them may proceed. It concerns a rental housing unit commonly known as 123 Main St., Los Angeles, CA, reportedly sold at a foreclosure sale on or about January 1, 2026, previously occupied by Jane Doe as tenant, with John Smith identified as the purchaser or successor in interest following that sale. Section 1161b does not itself use the phrase "bona fide tenant" as a defined statutory term; this sheet uses that commonly-used shorthand only to describe a tenant whose lease is not disqualified from the statute's protections under the specific conditions Section 1161b itself lists, which are described in the clauses below. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself serve, calculate the deadline for, or determine the adequacy of any notice to quit; it does not determine whether any specific tenancy is a month-to-month or periodic tenancy, is under a fixed-term lease, or falls within any exception this statute states; and it does not initiate, advance, or complete any unlawful detainer action concerning this or any other property.

THE 90-DAY NOTICE TO QUIT FOR A PERIODIC TENANCY AFTER A FORECLOSURE SALE
California Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b(a) requires that a tenant or subtenant in possession of a rental housing unit under a month-to-month lease or other periodic tenancy at the time the property is sold in foreclosure — such as the unit at 123 Main St., Los Angeles, CA, if Jane Doe's tenancy was on that basis — be given at least 90 days' written notice to quit, served under Code of Civil Procedure § 1162, before the tenant or subtenant may be removed from the property under this chapter's summary eviction procedure. The statute expressly states that this 90-day requirement applies "notwithstanding Section 1161a" — meaning it displaces, for this specific situation, the shorter notice period that Section 1161a would otherwise set for a tenant whose unit is sold in various other circumstances (execution sale, judicial foreclosure, private sale, and others), which is described in a companion clause of this sheet. Section 1161b(a) does not itself distinguish among 90-day-notice recipients based on the arm's-length, non-relative, or fair-market-rent conditions that Section 1161b(b) lists — those conditions instead govern a separate, additional protection available specifically to a fixed-term lease tenant, described elsewhere in this sheet.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Notwithstanding Section 1161a, a tenant or subtenant in possession of a rental housing unit under a month-to-month lease or periodic tenancy at the time the property is sold in foreclosure shall be given 90 days’ written notice to quit pursuant to Section 1162 before the tenant or subtenant may be removed from the property as prescribed in this chapter."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161b(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 1161b(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1161b.&lawCode=CCP)
  Known gap: This clause quotes Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b, subdivision (a) only, which is the sole citation for this clause. It does not address how the 90-day period is counted (calendar days versus court days, or whether weekends and holidays are excluded), which Section 1161b's text does not itself state and which this clause does not resolve. It does not address the separately-numbered statute governing how a written notice to quit under Section 1162 must be served (personal delivery, substituted service, or posting and mailing) — Section 1162's service mechanics are outside this clause's scope. It does not determine whether any specific tenancy is, in fact, a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, or whether a specific sale is, in fact, a foreclosure sale within the meaning of this statute.

THE GENERAL POST-SALE NOTICE PERIOD THIS STATUTE DISPLACES
Section 1161b's 90-day notice requirement operates against the backdrop of a separate, more general statute, California Code of Civil Procedure § 1161a, which governs removal of a person holding over after several kinds of post-sale transfers of real property — including, under Section 1161a(b)(3), property "sold in accordance with Section 2924 of the Civil Code, under a power of sale contained in a deed of trust," which is the nonjudicial trustee's-sale foreclosure process most California residential mortgage foreclosures use. Absent Section 1161b's specific 90-day carve-out, Section 1161a(c) would instead require only that a tenant or subtenant be given written notice to quit "at least as long as the term of hiring itself but not exceeding 30 days" before removal. Section 1161b's own text signals this relationship expressly, stating that its 90-day requirement applies "notwithstanding Section 1161a."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(3) Where the property has been sold in accordance with Section 2924 of the Civil Code, under a power of sale contained in a deed of trust executed by such person, or a person under whom such person claims, and the title under the sale has been duly perfected."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161a(b)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 1161a(b)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1161a.&lawCode=CCP)
  "(c) Notwithstanding the provisions of subdivision (b), a tenant or subtenant in possession of a rental housing unit which has been sold by reason of any of the causes enumerated in subdivision (b), who rents or leases the rental housing unit either on a periodic basis from week to week, month to month, or other interval, or for a fixed period of time, shall be given written notice to quit pursuant to Section 1162, at least as long as the term of hiring itself but not exceeding 30 days, before the tenant or subtenant may be removed therefrom as prescribed in this chapter."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161a(c) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 1161a(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1161a.&lawCode=CCP)
  Known gap: This clause cites two subdivisions of the same statutory section, Code of Civil Procedure § 1161a — subdivision (b)(3) (identifying a trustee's sale under Civil Code § 2924 as one of the causes Section 1161a covers) and subdivision (c) (the general notice-period rule, capped at 30 days, that would apply in the absence of Section 1161b) — grouped together because they together describe the general rule Section 1161b's 90-day requirement overrides for a foreclosure-sale tenant, not because they independently corroborate each other. This clause does not address Section 1161a's other enumerated causes (execution sale, judicial foreclosure, private sale, or a conditional sale contract default under Health and Safety Code § 18037.5), which involve property dispositions other than a nonjudicial foreclosure sale and so are outside the scope of a sheet about Section 1161b. It does not resolve whether Section 1161a's 30-day-or-term-of-hiring notice period, rather than Section 1161b's 90-day period, applies to any specific tenancy — that depends on whether the underlying sale was a foreclosure sale within Section 1161b's meaning, which this clause does not determine.

FIXED-TERM LEASE SURVIVAL AND ITS FOUR STATUTORY EXCEPTIONS
Beyond the 90-day notice requirement for a periodic tenancy, Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b(b) grants a distinct, additional protection to a tenant or subtenant holding possession under a fixed-term residential lease entered into before transfer of title at the foreclosure sale: such a lease-holding tenant "shall have the right to possession until the end of the lease term, and all rights and obligations under the lease shall survive foreclosure." That survival right is not absolute. The statute allows the tenancy to be terminated on 90 days' written notice to quit under subdivision (a) — the same 90-day period described elsewhere in this sheet, not a separate, shorter period — if any one of four listed conditions applies: the purchaser or successor in interest (such as John Smith) will occupy the unit as a primary residence; the lessee is the mortgagor or the mortgagor's child, spouse, or parent; the lease was not the result of an arm's-length transaction; or the lease requires rent substantially less than fair market rent for the property (unless that reduced or subsidized rent results from a federal, state, or local subsidy or law). Whether a fixed-term lease affecting 123 Main St., Los Angeles, CA is entitled to this survival protection, or instead falls within one of these four conditions, is not addressed by this sheet.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(b) In addition to the rights set forth in subdivision (a), tenants or subtenants holding possession of a rental housing unit under a fixed-term residential lease entered into before transfer of title at the foreclosure sale shall have the right to possession until the end of the lease term, and all rights and obligations under the lease shall survive foreclosure, except that the tenancy may be terminated upon 90 days’ written notice to quit pursuant to subdivision (a) if any of the following conditions apply: (1) The purchaser or successor in interest will occupy the housing unit as a primary residence. (2) The lessee is the mortgagor or the child, spouse, or parent of the mortgagor. (3) The lease was not the result of an arms’ length transaction. (4) The lease requires the receipt of rent that is substantially less than fair market rent for the property, except when rent is reduced or subsidized due to a federal, state, or local subsidy or law."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161b(b) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 1161b(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1161b.&lawCode=CCP)
  Known gap: This clause quotes Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b, subdivision (b) in its entirety, including its four numbered conditions — all part of a single statutory subdivision, not independent sources. The statute itself does not use the term "bona fide tenant" anywhere in this subdivision or elsewhere in Section 1161b; this sheet's introductory clause discloses that this sheet's use of that shorthand is not a quotation of statutory language. This clause does not address who bears the burden of proving whether one of the four disqualifying conditions applies (that burden-of-proof rule is addressed in a separate clause of this sheet, sourced to Section 1161b(c)), and it does not determine, for any specific lease, whether it was entered into before transfer of title at the foreclosure sale, whether any occupant is the mortgagor's relative, whether a given transaction was at arm's length, or what fair market rent for a specific unit is — all of which are factual questions this clause does not resolve.

BURDEN OF PROOF ON THE PURCHASER OR SUCCESSOR IN INTEREST
California Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b(c) places the burden of proof on the party seeking to remove a fixed-term lease tenant early: "The purchaser or successor in interest shall bear the burden of proof in establishing that a fixed-term residential lease is not entitled to protection under subdivision (b)." In other words, if John Smith, as purchaser or successor in interest for 123 Main St., Los Angeles, CA, contends that Jane Doe's fixed-term lease falls within one of the four disqualifying conditions described in subdivision (b) — owner-occupancy intent, a mortgagor-relative lessee, a non-arm's-length lease, or below-market rent not attributable to a subsidy — the statute assigns that party, not the tenant, the burden of proving it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(c) The purchaser or successor in interest shall bear the burden of proof in establishing that a fixed-term residential lease is not entitled to protection under subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161b(c) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 1161b(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1161b.&lawCode=CCP)
  Known gap: This clause quotes Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b, subdivision (c) only, a single subdivision distinct from, though textually dependent on, subdivision (b)'s four conditions quoted in a separate clause of this sheet. It does not address in which proceeding or forum this burden is applied (for example, as an issue litigated within an unlawful detainer action), what quantum of proof the statute requires, or how a specific dispute over whether a lease is entitled to subdivision (b) protection would be resolved — those procedural questions are not addressed by the statutory text this clause quotes.

TWO FURTHER STATUTORY LIMITS: A PARTY TO THE NOTE, AND LOCAL JUST-CAUSE ORDINANCES
Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b states two further limits on its own application. First, subdivision (d) provides that the entire section "shall not apply if any party to the note remains in the property as a tenant, subtenant, or occupant" — so an occupant who is, or remains, a party to the promissory note the foreclosed deed of trust secured is not within Section 1161b's protection, regardless of whether that occupancy is on a periodic or fixed-term basis. Second, subdivision (e) is an express savings clause: "Nothing in this section is intended to affect any local just cause eviction ordinance," and the section "does not, and shall not be construed to, affect the authority of a public entity that otherwise exists to regulate or monitor the basis for eviction." A city or county ordinance imposing its own just-cause-for-eviction requirements is therefore not preempted or altered by Section 1161b.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(d) This section shall not apply if any party to the note remains in the property as a tenant, subtenant, or occupant. (e) Nothing in this section is intended to affect any local just cause eviction ordinance. This section does not, and shall not be construed to, affect the authority of a public entity that otherwise exists to regulate or monitor the basis for eviction."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161b(d)-(e) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 1161b(d), (e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1161b.&lawCode=CCP)
  Known gap: This clause quotes Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b, subdivisions (d) and (e) together, as one contiguous passage of the same statutory section — they are grouped here because both operate as limits on Section 1161b's own application, not because they address the same subject matter as each other. Subdivision (d)'s reference to 'a party to the note' is not itself defined further within this section; this clause does not resolve who counts as a party to the note for a specific loan, or how that status is established. Subdivision (e) does not identify any specific local just-cause ordinance, and this sheet does not research or describe the just-cause or eviction-control ordinance, if any, of the city or county where the affected property is located — a reader would need to consult that jurisdiction's own ordinance separately. This clause also does not address the separate, statewide just-cause eviction and rent-cap statute (Civil Code § 1946.2, under AB 1482), which is the subject of a different information sheet elsewhere in this corpus and operates independently of Section 1161b.

CLOSING ACKNOWLEDGMENT
I have reviewed this information sheet describing California's statutory 90-day notice-to-quit requirement and fixed-term lease survival protection under Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b, as they may relate to the rental housing unit at 123 Main St., Los Angeles, CA. I understand that this document is informational only: it does not itself serve any notice to quit, does not determine whether any tenancy is periodic or fixed-term, does not determine whether any of Section 1161b's stated conditions or exceptions applies to Jane Doe's tenancy or John Smith's status as purchaser or successor in interest, and does not initiate, advance, or complete any unlawful detainer action.

Executed on January 1, 2026 at Los Angeles, California.
